meta.title: Godot Game Development for Kids and Teens: GDScript, 2D and 3D
meta.description: Godot game development course for ages 10 to 17: live online classes building real 2D and 3D games in Godot 4 with GDScript, from first scene to a finished web build.
keywords: game development classes for kids online
meta.level: Beginner to text coding, ages 10 to 17

program_overview.title: Godot Game Development for Kids and Teens
program_overview.tagline: A real game engine, a real scripting language, and games your child actually finishes.
program_overview.description:
Godot is a free and open source game engine released under the MIT license, so a student can download it, build anything, and keep everything they make, with no account, subscription or fee. It runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, and its own scripting language, GDScript, is designed to be easy to pick up for beginners while still being the language professional Godot developers use every day. That makes it the natural step for a child who has outgrown block coding and wants to write real code inside a real engine.

This 6-month live course is built around Godot 4. Students learn the engine's core idea first: everything is a node, nodes combine into scenes, and scenes combine into games. In the first two months they finish a complete 2D arcade game with a score, a game over screen and a restart button. Months three and four build a proper platformer with gravity, tile map levels, enemies, animation and sound. Month five moves into 3D, and month six is a capstone: each student designs, builds, playtests and exports a game of their own.

The course is taught live by a teacher who reads each student's code as they write it. Younger students build the core version of each project; older or faster students take the stretch features, so a 10-year-old and a 16-year-old are both working at the edge of what they can do. Every month ends with a playable game and a short assessment, so progress is something parents can see and play.
what_makes_this_different: Godot 4 and GDScript from the first week: real text code inside a real engine, not a toy editor
A finished, playable game every month, ending in a web build that family and friends can open in a browser
Engine ideas taught properly: nodes, scenes, signals and the physics process, so students understand why their game works
Core and stretch versions of every project, so ages 10 to 17 each work at the right level in the same course
Game feel treated as a skill: animation, sound, camera and juice are taught, not left to chance
A capstone where each student scopes, builds and playtests an original game from a written design document

learning_path.phase_1: Godot foundations and a first finished game: the editor, nodes and scenes, GDScript, movement, collisions, signals, a HUD and a web export
learning_path.phase_2: Platformers and game feel: CharacterBody2D physics, tile map levels, cameras, enemies with simple states, animation, sound and menus
learning_path.phase_3: 3D and the capstone: 3D scenes, lights and cameras, a 3D level, then an original game designed, built, playtested and exported

career_outcomes: A portfolio of at least five finished Godot games, from arcade to platformer to 3D
Confident GDScript: variables, functions, conditions, loops, arrays and signals used in real projects
An understanding of how game engines work that carries over to Unity, Unreal or any engine later
The habit of finishing: scoping a project, playtesting it and shipping a build others can play

phase_1_foundations_first_game.title: PHASE 1: Godot Foundations and a First Finished Game (Months 1-2, Weeks 1-8)
phase_1_foundations_first_game.description: Students learn how Godot thinks, write their first GDScript, and finish a complete 2D arcade game with scoring, a game over screen and a browser build.

week_1_2.title: Weeks 1-2: The Godot Editor and Your First Scene
topics: Installing Godot 4 and creating a first project
A tour of the editor: scene dock, inspector, viewport and file system
Nodes as building blocks and scenes as saved groups of nodes
Sprite2D, positions and the 2D coordinate system
Attaching a first GDScript and printing to the output panel
The _ready function and what happens when a scene starts
projects: Hello Godot: a scene with a moving title, a sprite and a script that greets the player by name
week_1_2.practice: Build three small scenes from memory and change one property of each from code

week_3_4.title: Weeks 3-4: Movement, Input and the Game Loop
topics: Variables, types and the @export annotation for values you tune in the inspector
The difference between _process and _physics_process, and why delta matters
Reading the keyboard with Input.get_axis and input actions
Velocity as speed with a direction, using Vector2
Keeping the player on screen with clamp
Reading error messages and fixing them calmly
projects: Top-down mover: a player ship that moves smoothly in eight directions and stays inside the screen
week_3_4.practice: Add a speed boost key and a slow-motion key, each tuned from the inspector
week_3_4.assessment: Month 1 check: build a moving player from a blank project and explain each line of the script

week_5_6.title: Weeks 5-6: Collisions, Signals and Spawning
topics: Area2D and collision shapes, and how Godot detects overlap
Signals: how one node tells another that something happened
Connecting signals in the editor and from code
Saving an enemy as its own scene and creating copies with instantiate
Timer nodes for spawning on a rhythm
Removing nodes safely with queue_free
projects: Dodge the falling objects: enemies spawn at random positions and the game reacts when the player is hit
week_5_6.practice: Add a second enemy type with a different speed and a different signal response

week_7_8.title: Weeks 7-8: Score, HUD, Game Over and Export
topics: A HUD on a CanvasLayer with Label and Button nodes
Keeping score and showing it on screen
Game states: title, playing and game over
Restarting the game cleanly
Adding sound effects with AudioStreamPlayer
Exporting a web build so the game runs in a browser
projects: First finished game: the dodge game with title screen, score, high score for the session, sound and a web build
week_7_8.practice: Playtest the game with two family members and fix the first two things they find confusing
week_7_8.assessment: Phase 1 assessment: a playable game handed in with a short written note on how signals connect its parts

phase_2_platformers_and_game_feel.title: PHASE 2: Platformers and Game Feel (Months 3-4, Weeks 9-16)
phase_2_platformers_and_game_feel.description: The genre that teaches the most: gravity, jumping, levels built from tiles, enemies that think a little, and the animation and sound that make a game feel alive.

week_9_10.title: Weeks 9-10: CharacterBody2D, Gravity and Jumping
topics: CharacterBody2D and why it suits a player character
Gravity as a steady change to velocity every physics frame
move_and_slide and checking is_on_floor before a jump
Variable jump height by releasing the jump key early
Coyote time and jump buffering as small kindnesses to the player
Using StaticBody2D for solid ground
projects: Jump lab: a test room where every jump setting can be tuned live and compared
week_9_10.practice: Write down three jump settings that feel good and three that feel bad, and explain the difference

week_11_12.title: Weeks 11-12: Tile Maps, Cameras and Animation
topics: Building levels with a TileSet and the TileMapLayer node
Adding collision to tiles so the player can stand on them
Camera2D that follows the player with smoothing and limits
AnimatedSprite2D for idle, run and jump animations
Choosing the right animation from the player's state in code
Collectibles and a level exit that loads the next scene
projects: Two-level platformer: tile map levels, collectibles, an animated player and a working exit
week_11_12.practice: Design a third level on paper first, then build it and count how many changes playtesting forced
week_11_12.assessment: Month 3 check: add a new mechanic, such as a double jump or a moving platform, to the platformer without help

month_4_enemies_and_polish.title: Month 4: Enemies, Menus and Game Feel

week_13_14.title: Weeks 13-14: Enemies and Simple State Machines
topics: An enemy that patrols between two points
States with an enum and the match statement: patrol, chase and hurt
Detecting the player with an Area2D vision zone
Health, damage and a short invincibility window after a hit
Knockback and a flash effect when something is hit
Groups as a simple way to find all enemies or all coins
projects: Enemy pack: three enemies with different behaviours added to the platformer
week_13_14.practice: Draw the state diagram for one enemy before coding it, then compare the code to the diagram

week_15_16.title: Weeks 15-16: Animation, Sound, Menus and Saving
topics: AnimationPlayer for doors, platforms and screen effects
Music and sound effects with volume set on audio buses
Main menu, pause menu and settings screen built from Control nodes
Changing scenes and passing information between them
Saving a best time or high score to a file with FileAccess
Particles for dust, sparkles and hits
projects: Polished platformer: menus, pause, music, particles and a saved best time, exported for the web
week_15_16.practice: Make a before and after video of the same level to show what game feel changes
week_15_16.assessment: Phase 2 assessment: the polished platformer plus a short live walkthrough of the enemy code

phase_3_3d_and_capstone.title: PHASE 3: 3D and the Capstone Game (Months 5-6, Weeks 17-24)
phase_3_3d_and_capstone.description: Students carry what they know into 3D, then design and ship an original game of their own, from written plan to playable build.

week_17_18.title: Weeks 17-18: 3D Scenes, Cameras and Movement
topics: Node3D, MeshInstance3D and the three axes
Lights, a WorldEnvironment and why a 3D scene looks flat without them
Camera3D that follows the player from behind
CharacterBody3D movement and jumping with Vector3
Collision shapes in 3D
Importing a simple 3D model in glTF format
projects: 3D playground: a lit scene where a character runs, jumps and pushes objects around
week_17_18.practice: Rebuild the 2D jump settings in 3D and note what had to change

week_19_20.title: Weeks 19-20: A 3D Collect-a-thon Level
topics: Designing a 3D level so the player can see where to go
Collectibles that spin, glow and play a sound
A timer and a finish gate
Simple 3D enemies that reuse the state machine from month 4
Keeping a 3D game running smoothly on an ordinary laptop
Exporting the 3D game for the web
projects: 3D level: collect every item before the timer runs out, with a finish screen and a best time
week_19_20.practice: Ask two people to play without instructions and note where they get lost
week_19_20.assessment: Month 5 check: a working 3D level and a short explanation of how it differs from the 2D projects

week_21_22.title: Weeks 21-22: Design Document, Scope and Prototype
topics: Writing a one-page game design document: idea, controls, goal and win and lose rules
Cutting scope so the game can be finished in three weeks
Building the core loop first and testing it ugly
Using placeholder art and swapping it later
Version control habits: saving numbered copies or using Git with the teacher
Peer playtesting with structured feedback
projects: Capstone prototype: the core loop of the student's own game, playable from start to finish
week_21_22.practice: Run a playtest with two people and write the three most useful pieces of feedback

week_23_24.title: Weeks 23-24: Polish, Export and Showcase
topics: Adding the menus, sound and effects the prototype skipped
Fixing the bugs found in playtesting, most important first
Exporting a web build and a desktop build
Writing a short game page: title, controls and credits
Presenting the game and the design decisions behind it
Where to go next: bigger Godot projects or our teen game development course
projects: Finished capstone game, exported and presented at the class showcase
week_23_24.practice: Write a short post-mortem: what went well, what you cut and what you would do next
week_23_24.assessment: Final assessment: the capstone game, the design document and a short code walkthrough with the teacher

faqs.question: What is Godot, and is it really free?
faqs.answer: Godot is a free and open source 2D and 3D game engine. It is released under the MIT license, which means there are no fees, no subscription and no royalties, and the games a student makes belong to them. It runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, and the course uses Godot 4.

faqs.question: Is Godot good for kids, or is it only for professionals?
faqs.answer: Both. Professional studios ship games with it, yet the editor is light, it installs in minutes, and its scripting language, GDScript, is designed to be easy to pick up for beginners. With a teacher guiding the first steps, children from about 10 handle it well, and the projects grow with them into the teen years.

faqs.question: What language does my child learn?
faqs.answer: GDScript, Godot's own scripting language. It reads a lot like Python, so the variables, functions, conditions, loops and arrays students learn here transfer directly to Python and other languages later. We teach GDScript rather than C# because it is the language Godot is built around and it can export games for the web.

faqs.question: My child is 10 and their cousin is 16. Can both take this course?
faqs.answer: Yes. Every project has a core version that every student finishes and stretch features for students who are older or faster, such as double jumps, extra enemy states or a saved high score. The teacher sets each student's stretch goals, so nobody is bored and nobody is lost.

faqs.question: How is this different from your other game development courses?
faqs.answer: Our Game Development for Kids course uses Scratch, Roblox and Minecraft, and our Game Development for Teens course uses Unity and C#. This course sits between them and is built entirely on Godot: real text code from the first week, but a lighter engine and a gentler language than Unity. Many students take it before moving on to the teen Unity course.

faqs.question: What will my child have built by the end?
faqs.answer: Six finished games: an arcade dodge game, a two-level platformer, an enemy pack, a polished platformer with menus and saving, a 3D collect-a-thon level, and an original capstone game with its own design document. Each one is exported so it can be played in a browser.

faqs.question: What computer do we need?
faqs.answer: A laptop or desktop running Windows, macOS or Linux, plus a stable internet connection for the live classes. Godot is a small free download, and the teacher helps with installation in the first class. Tablets and phones are not enough for building games.

faqs.question: Will my child's games be published online?
faqs.answer: Only if the family chooses. Students learn to make a web build that can be shared privately with family and friends. Uploading a game to a public site is optional and is always the parent's decision.

faqs.question: How are the classes run?
faqs.answer: Live online classes, twice a week, with a real teacher, in a group of 15 to 20 students, a mini batch of up to 6, or one to one. Current fees for your region are shown in the pricing section of this page.

faqs.question: Can we try a class first?
faqs.answer: Yes. Book a free demo class. The teacher builds a small piece of a Godot game with your child, sees where they are, and suggests whether group, mini batch or one-to-one classes fit best. There is no obligation to enrol.
